**`Hash.update(verifier)` throw analysis:**

Node.js `Hash.update(data)` accepts `string | Buffer | TypedArray | DataView`. For any string value — including empty strings, null bytes, Unicode surrogates, very long strings, binary content encoded as string — the call does NOT throw. Only non-accepted types (non-string, non-Buffer objects) cause `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`.

However: in Next.js route handlers, an uncaught synchronous exception is caught by the framework and returned as a 500 HTTP response — the process does not crash. The exception is "unhandled" at the application level but handled at the framework level.

**Does this matter for real-world standard OAuth usage?** RFC 6749 permits both `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and `multipart/form-data` for token endpoints. A deliberately crafted multipart request can trigger this path.
